title: Plants Per Row Calculator: Count Along the Row
description: Calculate how many plants fit in one row from its length and spacing with the Plants Per Row Calculator — garden rows to field rows. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a 100-foot row at 18-inch spacing holds 66 plants — or 67 if you plant both ends, a one-plant argument every gardener has had with a calculator.
quick_answer: The Plants Per Row Calculator divides a row's length by the in-row spacing to give the number of plants that row holds. Enter the row length and the spacing and read the count — for seed packets, transplant trays and bed planning, with the end-plant convention explained rather than hidden.
steps_intro: Length ÷ spacing — plus one old argument about the ends:

body.t: A 4 × 8 ft raised bed is three 8-ft rows of lettuce at 8-inch spacing: 12 per row, 36 per bed. The calculator turns seed-packet optimism into a layout. Whole-field populations scale up through the
Rows × plants per row = seedlings to start, plus the nursery's customary overage. Trays come in fixed cells; the row count decides how many to sow.
A 600-ft vine row at 8-ft spacing is 75 vines — trellis posts, drippers and replacements all derive from the same count.
Seed monitors promise a spacing; the row count over a measured run is the ground truth the monitor is audited against at the field's edge.

examples.label: Example · The ends argument, settled honestly

body.t: 100 ft at 18-in spacing: 100 ÷ 1.5 = 66.7 spaces. Planting strictly inside gives 66 plants; planting a plant at position zero and every 18 inches thereafter gives 67 with the last at 99 ft. Both conventions are defensible — the calculator uses full spaces (66) and this example names the difference.
A half-mile row (2,640 ft) of corn at 6.9-in spacing holds about 4,591 plants — the per-row view of the 30,303-per-acre population, useful when a single row's seed tube is the unit of failure.

popular_table.note: Fractional remainders are dropped — a row cannot hold two-thirds of a plant, and the shortfall collects at the row's end, where the headland forgives it.

faq: Why does my count differ by one from the calculator?

The end-plant convention: starting a plant at the very start of the row adds one whenever the division is exact or the gardener cheats the last spacing. The FAQ example shows both counts; pick the convention your planting actually follows.

Real rows start and end inside the field — headland room for turning, or the bed's frame. Subtract your end margins from the row length before dividing; the calculator assumes the length you give is plantable.
Count each line separately: a bed with two lines is two rows sharing a length. The per-row number stays honest; the bed total is rows × per-row.
Drip emitter spacing instead of plants?
Same division — emitters per line is how drip layouts are counted, and plant-per-emitter is the design rule the count feeds.
Staggering changes the pattern along neighbouring rows, not the count within one row — this page's number stands; the field page prices the density gain.
Rows on a slope or curve?
Use the row's true length along the ground or curve, not its map projection — a curved row at the field's edge can run several percent longer than its chord.
Packet counts vary by variety; weigh or count a sample to calibrate seeds-per-gramme, then the row count becomes a weight at the kitchen scale's resolution.
